cards.title: Subquadratic factor-three edit-distance approximation
cards.area: Approximation algorithms and hardness of approximation
cards.formal: Does there exist a classical randomized algorithm and constants \(\eta>0\) and \(C>0\) such that, for every pair of explicitly given strings \(X,Y\) of total length \(n\), the algorithm runs in at most \(C(n+2)^{2-\eta}\) time and, with probability at least \(2/3\), outputs an estimate \(\widehat d\) satisfying \[\operatorname{ED}(X,Y)\leq\widehat d\leq3\operatorname{ED}(X,Y)?\]

cards.why: Tests how much accuracy can be retained while obtaining a fixed polynomial speedup for a basic sequence-comparison problem. It separates the power of approximation from the quadratic barrier for exact computation, with relevance to algorithms for aligning and comparing strings.
cards.status_note: Read the complete original introductory question and its full author counterpart, the Andoni–Nosatzki full-version main theorem, the Goldenberg–Rubinstein–Saha ordinary-input result, and the full March 2026 paper’s tradeoff table and Theorem 6.1. Verified the STOC 2026 publisher date. Searches through 12 September 2026 found no fixed-power-time factor-three resolution. The sequential model and constant success probability make explicit the randomized algorithmic target; no near-linear-time requirement is imposed.

sentences: The task compares two arbitrary explicit strings using unit-cost insertions, deletions and substitutions.
The estimate must lie between the true edit distance and three times that distance.
The algorithm must save a fixed positive power over quadratic time on every input.
Known truly subquadratic algorithms approach factor three from above.
The 2026 approximation scheme achieves better accuracy, but its proved time saving is smaller than a fixed power of the input length.

cards.definitions:
The unit-cost Levenshtein edit distance \(\operatorname{ED}(X,Y)\) is the minimum number of single-character insertions, deletions and substitutions needed to transform \(X\) into \(Y\). Each operation costs one, including substitution. There are no transpositions, moves of blocks, or cheaper substitution costs. The two strings can have different lengths or be empty.

The input consists of both strings in full, with their lengths. Let \(n=|X|+|Y|\). Characters can be encoded by integer labels in \(\{1,\ldots,\max\{1,n\}\}\); only equality of labels matters. This allows arbitrary alphabets occurring in the input, rather than a binary-alphabet promise. Renaming polynomially bounded integer symbols takes only a near-linear preprocessing cost, which is included.

Use the usual sequential random-access model with \(O(\log(n+2))\)-bit words: a word read or write, comparison, Boolean operation, shift, or arithmetic operation on a constant number of words costs one step. Memory is initially empty except for the input; reading the input, all preprocessing and writing the output are charged. The algorithm has independent fair random bits, but no advice or uncharged preprocessed strings, distance oracle, parallel processors or quantum operations.

One uniform algorithm and fixed constants must work at every input length, for every input pair and every distance regime. Its running-time bound holds for every random tape. The probability of meeting the approximation guarantee is over its internal randomness alone; the inputs need not be random or generated by a mutation model.

The estimate may be an integer: rounding a valid nonnegative rational estimate down preserves the inequalities because the true distance is an integer. No edit script or alignment has to be returned. When the strings are identical, a successful estimate must be exactly zero.

Truly subquadratic means a fixed positive exponent saving \(\eta\), independent of \(n\). A bound such as \(n^{2}/\log n\), or a stated improvement of the form \(n^{2}/2^{(\log n)^{c}}\) with fixed \(0<c<1\), does not supply such a saving. A polylogarithmic overhead on an already fixed-power saving can be absorbed by decreasing \(\eta\).

The approximation factor is at most three, uniformly over the input size. A guarantee of \(3+\varepsilon\) for every fixed positive \(\varepsilon\), or \(3+o(1)\), does not itself establish this endpoint. The main question is existence of some positive runtime saving, not its optimal value.
cards.answer_criterion: Give an algorithm meeting the factor-three guarantee and some fixed positive exponent saving for all inputs in the stated model, or prove that no such randomized algorithm exists. State any hypothesis of a conditional negative result explicitly. An arbitrary constant approximation, a factor exceeding three, an average-case result, or a subpolynomial rather than fixed-power runtime saving is insufficient.

context_blocks.title: A constant factor in near-linear time is already known
context_blocks.text: Andoni and Nosatzki obtain \(O(n^{1+\gamma})\) time for every fixed \(\gamma>0\), with an approximation constant depending on \(\gamma\). Their theorem does not bound that constant by three. This is the known result preceding the source’s truncated question.

context_blocks.title: The approximation endpoint remains a distinction
context_blocks.text: Goldenberg, Rubinstein and Saha obtain a \(3+o(1)\) approximation in \(n^{1.6+o(1)}\) time without preprocessing. Despite the paper’s title, this is a result in the ordinary input model. Its approximation factor approaches three from above and therefore does not certify the exact factor-three guarantee.

context_blocks.title: The 2026 advance improves accuracy with a smaller time saving
context_blocks.text: Mao and Rubinstein give a randomized \((1+\varepsilon)\)-approximation for every fixed \(\varepsilon>0\), in time \(n^{2}/2^{(\log n)^{\Omega(1)}}\), with high probability. The demonstrated saving is subpolynomial in \(n\). Their theorem crosses the factor-three accuracy threshold but does not establish \(O(n^{2-\eta})\) time for any fixed \(\eta>0\).

context_blocks.title: The source’s new metric is a separate subject
context_blocks.text: The original paper also studies edit distance with cheaper substitutions and bicriteria guarantees involving substitution and insertion/deletion budgets. Those positive results concern a different cost model or additional parameters. The selected introductory question uses ordinary unit-cost distance on unrestricted inputs.

cards.context:
Andoni and Nosatzki obtain \(O(n^{1+\gamma})\) time for every fixed \(\gamma>0\), with an approximation constant depending on \(\gamma\). Their theorem does not bound that constant by three. This is the known result preceding the source’s truncated question.

Goldenberg, Rubinstein and Saha obtain a \(3+o(1)\) approximation in \(n^{1.6+o(1)}\) time without preprocessing. Despite the paper’s title, this is a result in the ordinary input model. Its approximation factor approaches three from above and therefore does not certify the exact factor-three guarantee.

Mao and Rubinstein give a randomized \((1+\varepsilon)\)-approximation for every fixed \(\varepsilon>0\), in time \(n^{2}/2^{(\log n)^{\Omega(1)}}\), with high probability. The demonstrated saving is subpolynomial in \(n\). Their theorem crosses the factor-three accuracy threshold but does not establish \(O(n^{2-\eta})\) time for any fixed \(\eta>0\).

The original paper also studies edit distance with cheaper substitutions and bicriteria guarantees involving substitution and insertion/deletion budgets. Those positive results concern a different cost model or additional parameters. The selected introductory question uses ordinary unit-cost distance on unrestricted inputs.

meta.status_scope: No claim of exhaustive open-status verification
methodology: Detailed cards have individually written statements, context, significance, and documented results. Source notes are unfinished research records and do not yet meet that standard. The legacy index is retained for traceability.
Open in the source means open at the date of that source. The build date, 10 September 2026, does not establish current open status. Old excerpts may omit conditions or subsequent results.

Selection considers model power, necessary resources, sharp bounds, structural characterizations, explicit constructions, and minimal assumptions. Source notes use a heuristic screen; detailed cards give an individual explanation.

The earlier automatic paper screen allowed at most one new card per paper title and rejected identical formulations and close duplicates within a source. Approved textbook and survey imports retain multiple distinct questions per publication. Confirmed overlaps supplement existing cards; collection-wide semantic deduplication remains incomplete.

Short quotations retain the source language. Later related literature, where listed, is a research aid rather than evidence of resolution. Personal notes and saved cards are stored locally in your browser.

Textbook and survey questions are dated paraphrases; source locations, conjectures, research directions and caveats are preserved on the problem cards. These annotations do not establish current open status or change a later card review. New source drafts remain unassessed for importance. The reader contains the imported questions and external bibliographic references only; source files are not bundled.

Selection groups follow the agreed 10 large and 25 small categories. Our primary goal is a benchmark of 500 problems. Top 100 is a priority subset of those same 500, with secondary editorial attention. Both use the same category order and the same ranking within each category. The existing Top 1000 view is not an active benchmark goal. The respective prefixes are 5/2, 25/10 and 50/20 problems per large/small category. The legacy Top 1000 view has 1000 assigned places and 0 reserved places. Each card records its category explicitly. These counts describe saved candidates; classification does not verify a statement or its current open status. Deleted records are absent from the catalogue and exports. Their stable IDs and reasons are retained to prevent reimport. Final quota selection and a comprehensive deduplication audit remain pending.

Importance ordering is an editorial assessment of foundational significance, breadth of consequences, and influence on other questions. Each assessed card gives a reason. The category-wide review also uses shared priority bands for questions of comparable scope; it does not claim that these ties have a scientifically meaningful internal order. Unassessed drafts share a provisional score of 50; their relative order is only an ID tie-break, not an importance judgment. The first 5/2 places in each large/small category are an explicit editorial focus selection balancing importance and topical diversity. Focus ordering does not alter importance scores; remaining candidates use score and ID order. The primary target is 500 problems; Top 100 is its priority subset with secondary editorial attention. Top 100, Top 500 and the legacy Top 1000 view use the first 5/2, 25/10 and 50/20 category places respectively, all from the same ranking. Category positions include all candidates and remain fixed when filtering. Publication date, source date, and card detail do not increase importance. Records marked resolved are placed after the remaining candidates, without changing their historical importance score. Importance review does not establish that a saved question is still open.
